summary: Describes two mappings of syslog to TCP connections, both useful for reliable delivery of event messages.

eli5.summary: It sends diary notes by a method that makes sure each note gets there.

questions: what is the syslog raw profile
subtitle: Two ways to carry syslog messages over BEEP on TCP, so event logs arrive reliably, authenticated and optionally encrypted.

tldr.problem: The usual UDP-based syslog gives no assurance that event messages arrive, and no built-in authentication or encryption.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two BEEP profiles over TCP: RAW, which carries the existing syslog text format, and COOKED, which wraps each entry in XML with identity and path information and acknowledges it.
tldr.outcome: Both profiles inherit ordered, reliable delivery from BEEP, and SASL and TLS can add authentication and privacy. BEEP does not provide object integrity, so a compromised device or relay can still alter logs undetected.

today: RFC 3195 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 3080 (BEEP) and RFC 3164 (BSD syslog).

sections.title: Reliable Syslog over BEEP
sections.content:
The syslog protocol (RFC 3164) offers a spectrum of service options for network event logging. This RFC describes how to realize syslog when reliable delivery is required. It does not argue for or against using reliable delivery.

It defines two profiles of BEEP (RFC 3080), a framework for connection-oriented, asynchronous interactions that provides authentication, privacy and retransmission-based reliability. The RAW profile is a high-performance, low-impact mapping using essentially the same format as UDP syslog. The COOKED profile uses a structured entry format in which individual entries are acknowledged, positively or negatively. At the time of writing the only BEEP transport mapping is BEEP over TCP (RFC 3081), and all mappings must deliver the messages of a channel reliably and in order, so both profiles deliver reliably.
sections.eli5: There are two ways to hand over the log notes: a quick way that copies the old note style, and a careful way that fills in a form for every note.

sections.title: Devices, Relays and Collectors
sections.content:
The model has three roles. Devices create syslog entries, collectors receive them, and a relay accepts entries from devices and other relays and forwards them to collectors and other relays. The device and collector relationship can be many-to-many, and more than one relay may sit between a device and a collector.

Relays are useful for administrative reasons (for example as an application proxy on a firewall or one per department that authenticates its devices), for filtering, and for converting formats. A role applies only to a particular BEEP channel, so one server can be a device, relay and collector all at once, even to the same peer over different channels of one session. The choice of profile is independent of role: a device-to-relay link could use RAW while the relay-to-collector link uses COOKED.

Devices and relays MAY discover relays and collectors with DNS SRV, using service syslog and protocol tcp, though resource-limited devices or restrictive networks may make DNS inappropriate.
sections.eli5: Think of a school mail system. Kids write notes (devices), the office passes them along (relays), and the principal files them (the collector). One person can play several of these jobs.

sections.title: The RAW Profile
sections.content:
The RAW profile is designed for minimal implementation effort, efficiency and backward compatibility, especially where legacy syslog processing applies. It is identified as http://xml.resource.org/profiles/syslog/RAW, uses a MIME type of application/octet-stream and supplies no data during channel creation.

Once the channel is open, the listener sends a first MSG saying it is ready to be a syslog sink. That message has no semantics and is ignored. The initiator then sends one or more syslog entries in the UDP format as ANS replies, and finishes with a NUL reply and closes the channel. Each message MUST follow Section 4 of RFC 3164 and have a facility, severity and text, and relays MUST follow its Section 4.2.2.

The overhead of one ANS frame is about thirty octets. To reduce it, several messages can share one frame, separated by CRLF. Each message body MUST be 1024 bytes or less, and there MUST NOT be a CRLF between the last message and the frame's END trailer.
sections.eli5: RAW is like reading your notes aloud one after another over a phone that never drops. The listener says hello, you read your notes, then say "that's all".

sections.title: The COOKED Profile Elements
sections.content:
The COOKED profile, identified as http://xml.resource.org/profiles/syslog/COOKED, is aimed at new implementations and allows finer tagging and more automation, at the cost of more overhead. Its messages use application/beep+xml and it has three elements. Initiators send them in MSG messages, and the listener answers with ok in a RPY or error in an ERR.

  • iam identifies the sender: its type (device, relay or collector), fully qualified domain name and an IP address. The listener accepts or rejects it, for example when authentication is inadequate or the user may not act in that role, and most installations are expected to require an iam before accepting any entry. It can also be embedded in the channel start element.
  • entry carries one parsed syslog entry with attributes facility, severity, timestamp, hostname and tag, plus optional deviceFQDN, deviceIP, pathID and xml:lang. The original message text MUST be preserved exactly in its character data.
  • path lists the relays an entry passed through, with the properties of each link.

When a relay gets a message without a valid priority, timestamp or hostname, it follows the RFC 3164 rules, treats the facility and severity as 8 and 6, uses the device name it knows, and sets the timestamp to the time received. An entry can be rejected if no iam was accepted, if the user lacks authority to generate or relay it, or if its pathID refers to an unknown path.
sections.eli5: COOKED is a form with boxes: who I am, what the note says and what kind it is, and which desks it passed through. Every form gets a "got it" or "no, because..." back.

sections.title: Paths and Link Properties
sections.content:
A path element describes the chain of relays that entries passed through. An empty path identifies a device, and a path containing another path identifies a relay. Each has a pathID (digits, unique on its channel), fromIP and toIP (MUST be given), optional fromFQDN and toFQDN, and a linkprops string of single-character flags. Later entry elements point at a path through their own pathID.

On receiving a path, a peer MUST check that the from and to addresses match the transport connection, that the flags match the session, and that the pathID is unique on the channel. If all pass, it answers ok; otherwise it returns an error. If nested paths name the receiving machine, that may indicate a routing loop. Most of the complexity falls on relays: devices never need to generate paths, and collectors only verify and log them.
sections.eli5: A path is like a stamp trail on a letter showing every post office it went through, and whether each leg was locked, watched or safe.

sections.title: Authentication, Privacy and Security Limits
sections.content:
Because the profiles run over BEEP, security is layered on the BEEP session. To stop inauthentic, replayed or altered messages, peers should be configured to require a strong authentication technology, and implementations SHOULD use the SASL mechanism DIGEST-MD5 (RFC 2831) for authentication, replay protection and integrity. To prevent observation, implementations SHOULD use the BEEP TLS profile with the cipher TLS_RSA_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA, although volume and timing of traffic remain visible. BEEP identities SHOULD match the FQDN of the initiating peer.

The RFC is frank about the limit: BEEP secures communication but not object integrity. A compromised device may generate incorrect messages undetectably, and relays and collectors can modify, insert or delete messages undetectably, so other techniques are needed to make that detectable.
sections.eli5: The delivery truck can be locked and checked, but if someone inside the post office changes a letter, the lock on the truck does not help.

sections.title: Registrations and Error Codes
sections.content:
The RFC registers both profiles and allocates a single well-known TCP port, 601, for syslog-conn. Whether COOKED or RAW is in use is negotiated in-band. It selects the IANA URIs http://iana.org/beep/SYSLOG/RAW and http://iana.org/beep/SYSLOG/COOKED.

It also lists reply codes used in error elements, among them 200 success, 530 authentication required, 535 authentication failure, 537 action not authorized for user and 554 transaction failed, such as a policy violation. The RFC includes a DTD defining the iam, entry and path elements.
sections.eli5: Port 601 is the front door for this kind of log delivery, and the error codes are the polite reasons the doorman gives when he says no.

viz.caption: LINKPROPS FLAGS IN A PATH ELEMENT

items.label: Weak privacy
items.desc: Encryption with less than 80 bits of key.

items.label: Strong privacy
items.desc: Encryption with 80 bits or more of key, or a transfer that cannot be eavesdropped.

items.label: User authenticated
items.desc: A valid user was authenticated via SASL or TLS and an iam was accepted.

items.label: Authenticated source
items.desc: An authentication layer authenticates the source of every entry.

items.label: Replay protected
items.desc: The link is protected against message replay.

items.label: Integrity
items.desc: The link is protected against modification of messages in passing.

items.label: Device
items.desc: The from side of the link is a device.
